svg.title: Write-Ahead Log
svg.desc: Write-Ahead Log. Log each change before applying it, so a commit survives a crash, recovery replays the log, and replicas and backups follow it. Step 1, No log: force every page: Without a log, COMMIT must force 8 pages into 7 files, and a crash mid-write can tear a page. Step 2, Log first, pages later: Each change appends a WAL record; COMMIT flushes the log to 0/7600C308, and the pages stay dirty. Step 3, Replay after a crash: A crash wipes memory; recovery replays the WAL from the redo point, and a standby replays it too. Step 4, What durability costs: Each commit waits for one WAL flush; page images swell WAL after checkpoints. InnoDB does the same.

g.text: Without a log, COMMIT must force 8 pages into 7 files, and a crash mid-write can tear a page.
Each change appends a WAL record; COMMIT flushes the log to 0/7600C308, and the pages stay dirty.
A crash wipes memory; recovery replays the WAL from the redo point, and a standby replays it too.
Each commit waits for one WAL flush; page images swell WAL after checkpoints. InnoDB does the same.
With no log, a commit is only
changed is on disk, and a crash
in between leaves half of it.
The 8 pages never reached disk before
the crash: replaying the WAL rebuilt
them, then a checkpoint wrote them.
(256 MB here). Checksums are on by
default since 18, so the first hint-bit
change to a page after a checkpoint
Measured with pgbench on a laptop,
10 s per run: round the numbers.
COMMIT has to put every changed
page on disk before it returns:
· 8 pages of 8 kB, in 7 different files
· each one written at its own offset
A checkpoint that wrote one such order
took 6–7 ms, every commit would wait.
Power fails mid-write: a torn page,
Nothing in the data files can repair it.
crash after 4 of 8 writes: the items are on disk, their order isn’t
page 5057 on disk: 90 rows, LSN 0/64A3FE20 · in memory: 91 rows
page 5057 on disk after recovery: 91 rows, LSN 0/76008280
time, one run on a laptop
receives each record as it is written and replays it:
base backup + archived WAL → any point in time
with wal_level = logical, a replication slot
turns the same records into row changes
COMMIT WAITS FOR A WAL FLUSH
pgbench, 10 s per run, one order per transaction
off may lose the last ≤ 3 × wal_writer_delay of
commits in a crash, but never corrupts the data
first order after CHECKPOINT · 7 page images
1,238 page images in those first 10 s, 36% of the WAL:
mostly customers and products pages the FK checks locked
One starts every checkpoint_timeout, or sooner if
max_wal_size would fill, and paces its writes to
end at 0.9 of the interval. One timed checkpoint:
writes spread over 270 s of the 300 s interval
Fewer checkpoints: fewer page images and less I/O,
but more WAL to replay after a crash.
redo log: its WAL, 32 files in #innodb_redo,
writes and flushes the log at every commit;
2 or 0 flush it about once a second instead.
doublewrite buffer: each 16 kB page goes to a
.dblwr file first, then to its place, so a torn
page is restored from that copy; PostgreSQL
restores it from the page image in its WAL.
Defaults read from a MySQL 8.4.11 server.
